svg.title: A log record's journey through the four objects, showing every place it can be dropped and why it can appear twice
svg.desc: A static architecture diagram of the Python logging module in three bands. The first band follows one call into the logger it was made on: the logger's effective level is checked first and a rejected record is never created; then a LogRecord is built; then the logger's own filters run. The second band walks the record up the dotted hierarchy from myapp.loader to myapp to root, emitting it from every handler it passes, and notes that ancestors' levels are not re-checked and ancestors' filters are not applied at all. The third band opens one handler: the handler's own level is checked, then the handler's filters run, then the formatter renders the line, then it is written to a destination. A panel at the foot lists the five places a record can disappear with no error raised, explains the duplicate message, and gives the rule for where a redacting filter must be attached.
svg.text: Where a log line goes, and every place it can vanish without a word
Four objects, and they are separate on purpose: a LOGGER decides whether to make a record, a FILTER decides and may edit, a HANDLER sends it somewhere, a FORMATTER renders it.
Red marks a point where the record disappears and NO error is raised. That silence is deliberate: a logging call that raised would take your program down at the worst possible moment.
1. Inside the logger you called
the call
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)
log.info("kept %d of %d", 4, 6)
GATE 1 — the logger's level
isEnabledFor(INFO)? The level is inherited from
the nearest ancestor that sets one; NOTSET means
"ask my parent", and the root's default is WARNING.
DROPPED — and no record
was even built. Cheapest exit.
the LogRecord is created
msg = "kept %d of %d" args = (4, 6)
levelno, name, created, pathname, lineno,
exc_info, plus anything from extra=
GATE 2 — this logger's filters
Return False to drop. Editing the record on the
way through is allowed, which is what makes
redaction possible at all.
DROPPED — a filter said no.
Nothing is written anywhere.
These filters run ONLY for calls made on THIS logger.
A record arriving from a child logger skips them entirely.
2. Up the dotted hierarchy
myapp.loader
handlers: none — so nothing is written here
propagate is True
myapp
handlers: 1 — WRITES A LINE
its LEVEL is not re-checked; its FILTERS are not run
propagate is True
root
handlers: 1 — WRITES THE SAME LINE AGAIN
basicConfig() put this one here, quietly
One call, two lines. THIS is the duplicate-message problem.
3. Inside one handler
Every handler the record passes runs all of this,
independently, with its own settings.
GATE 3 — the handler's level
The second of the two level checks, and the one
people forget. A logger at DEBUG with a handler
at WARNING emits no debug output, ever.
DROPPED by THIS handler —
others may still emit it.
GATE 4 — the handler's filters
A filter here sees EVERYTHING that reaches this
destination, from anywhere in the tree. This is
where a redacting filter belongs.
the formatter renders the line
msg % args happens HERE, not at the call site —
which is what lazy formatting buys you. The
TRACEBACK is rendered here too, after every
filter has already run.
a destination
stdout · a rotating file · syslog · a queue ·
an SMTP server · anything you subclass
Five places a line disappears, in order
1. the logger's level rejected it
2. a filter on that logger returned False
3. an ancestor had propagate = False
4. the handler's own level rejected it
5. a filter on that handler returned False
— and a sixth: there is no handler anywhere, so
the last-resort handler prints WARNING and above
to stderr and silently drops the rest.
Two fixes for the duplicate
propagate = False — right for a LIBRARY, whose
records must not escape into an application.
Handlers in one place only — right for an
APPLICATION, because there is then one thing to change.
The rule this diagram exists to make obvious
Levels are checked TWICE, on two different objects,
and both have to pass. Filters are checked twice too,
but the two are NOT equivalent:
a filter on a logger runs only for calls made on that
logger — never for records propagating up from a child.
Since every module calls getLogger(__name__) and is
therefore a descendant, a redacting filter on the top
logger protects almost nothing while looking like it
protects everything. Put it on each HANDLER.
And note where the traceback is rendered: in the
formatter, after every filter. A secret inside an
exception message walks past a filter untouched, so
scrub in the formatter as well — or, better, never put
a credential in an exception message.

Both surprising behaviours above were measured on Python 3.14.0 while this lesson was written, and the lab's test suite asserts them, so a future change fails the build rather than quietly making this picture wrong.
